utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Before we hear the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one matter I'd like to raise. Present in court now is Mr. Asim Dzambasovic, who is a team member and an investigator in the Halilovic team. Mr. Dzambasovic is not going to be in court for most of trial because it's likely that he'll be a witness in the Defence case. But we would like him to be present in court because this witness who is now coming, Mr. Gusic, is a witness who is going to give some evidence, although it's not limited to technical evidence, because he will give some technical sort of evidence and evidence relating to the construction of particular orders and documents. And for that reason, we would seek that Mr. Dzambasovic be present here because it's likely his evidence would bear on those sort of matters, bearing in mind that the Prosecution case includes an element of de jure command responsibility attributed to Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No objections to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there's one other -- well, two other preliminary matters before the witness comes: One of them is that my learned friend has sought leave to lead in relation to preliminary matters, and I've indicated that I have no difficulty with that at all in line of with what Your Honour said yesterday. And secondly, there is a matter of exhibits that are not yet admitted as exhibits. There is outstanding litigation in relation to those. And the Prosecution might seek to make clear what position they intend to take with respect to leading those documents when they're not currently admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Which documents are you particularly in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In particular, I have in mind a report by Nusret Sahic. It's the last -- I think it's 0165, Your Honour. The last -- 166, I'm sorry. I think that the Court has not ruled on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Pending Your Honours' decision on the -- on our motion for our exhibit list, I would suggest that Your Honours accept that as a mark for identification, subject on which Your Honours will eventually rule. The translation has been provided to -- to the Defence, and it is a pending motion, Your Honour. We do confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And when did you furnish this document to the Defence party? Do you have any record -- any signatures from Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've -- I've seen it. We got the translation two or three days ago. I don't want to suggest that I'd be prejudiced by the information in it. The question is really one of whether it's to be admitted now in advance of the ruling. We maintain, of course, an objection to it, but I won't be caught by surprise by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there's no present danger for the prejudice to your team, so I think there's no problem for us to allow this document to be used in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's -- perhaps I should be clear that we don't say there's no prejudice in our submission. What we say is that I'm not prejudiced by the element of surprise. We may be prejudiced in other ways. May I put my submission about it, that it's a document which in my submission ought not to go through this witness in any event. There's another witness coming, Nermin Eminovic, to whom that document more or less directly relates, and it would be more appropriate for the -- for that document to go through that witness if this Tribunal permits it to go in at all. So that therefore you're not -- the Tribunal is not put in an embarrassing position if the matter is just deferred for that witness. And that's the submission I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, your practice directions in this matter are quite clear, that all exhibits will be entered into evidence subject to later on any authentic arguments based on authenticity. And at that point Your Honours will rule on it. And this is not going to be ruled on until the end of the trial in any event. So this witness can certainly identify the document and it can be marked for identification and even as -- I'll go as far to say tendered as an exhibit. But as Your Honour said, that's something which you will always rule on later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you mix the two things together. At this moment, I would like you to submit to us this document as early as possible so maybe during breaks we will read this and decide whether there's any substantial prejudice to the Defence team. Then later on we'll decide whether you are going to use it or not. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's clear. Thank you. There's just one other matter I should raise, and it's a matter of concern. Given the way that the e-court is here set up -- Your Honour, given the -- the way in which the e-court is proceeding here, it was to be hoped that Mr. Halilovic would be in a position to see in B/C/S such exhibits or potential exhibits as were going to the witness. Now, because of the use of the Sanction process, I'm instructed that that cannot occur. We were given some notice by the Prosecutor of this in the past, but our resources -- it's not the Tribunal's problem, frankly, but I can indicate our resources don't extend to the photocopying of many documents for the accused man to read at this stage, bearing in mind that Mr. Gusic has come on relatively quickly and the Tribunal has admitted that, of course. Now, I don't know what the remedy is, and there's no remedy today, and I don't ask for there to be an adjournment. But I want there to be a remedy in the future, because it's a very difficult situation for Mr. Halilovic in a command responsibility case with technical evidence which is going to start today. It's -- it creates an unfairness to him. It's one that we think we can carry today, so we don't ask for the matter to be adjourned. I would be put in the position of having to seek adjournments and delays in the future if nothing can be done. I mention it now and hopefully goodwill will prevail and discussions can take place, but it's a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for bringing these matters to my attention. You know, I'm also new to this e-court, you know, system and technically speaking if the witness could see the B/C/S version on the monitor, there's no reason that your client could not. But anyway, we'll see to it, to find a way to solve this problem as early as possible so as to avoid any undue delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May I -- I would like to make the Prosecution's position very clear in this respect. Now, Mr. -- Defence counsel were alerted that there are about 23 documents which we are going to refer to today, so there's only 23. And the B/C/S version has been provided to the Defence for this very purpose. And therefore, they should be able to have got these 23 documents and shown them to the accused prior to today. As we are every single time we're going to use documents, we are allowing -- alerting the Defence to which documents we're going to use. They do have the B/C/S. We've gone to all the trouble to provide these documents. And it would be more -- more efficient for them to -- to bring them to court themselves because this e-court, as we said, is all new. We don't know whether we'll be able to put up the B/C/S version as well as the English on Sanction. And last time, Your Honours, when we did the split screen, you -- you could not actually read it. So these are some of the problems which we'll have to solve. And I think it's important that the Defence also try to cooperate in this matter and bring their documents in B/C/S for their client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. We note that is your position. But I believe there should be some improvement in the e-court system, and I mainly regard Mr. Morrissey's remarks is addressing to the court management, rather than to the other party. Well, I also have some matters which -- mainly concerning with the housekeeping issues; that is, the Prosecution asked for leave to disclose the four statements of several witnesses. In order to enable the Trial Chamber and the Defence to access the content of statement in relation to any prejudice to the Defence, the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecution to disclose the statements to Defence and the Trial Chamber as early as possible. The Trial Chamber has already received those statements. I wonder whether the Defence has received them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: These being the statements arising out of Ramiz Delalic? The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's about four statements. One is -- one witness statement is about the Selmo Cikotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And another is Ahmet Salihamidzic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have that bundle, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. I just want to make sure of that. And could we go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: There is one other matter, with your permission which I would like to raise, and that is with respect to exhibits again. Your Honour, it would be inefficient for the Prosecution to the prove the authenticity of every single document. And we feel to that end if the Defence could indicate to us - and this is something we have asked the Defence on several occasions - as to which exhibits they intend to dispute the authenticity of. Then the Prosecution could make preparations to prove those. But for us to prove every single one, it is certainly inefficient, and it is an obligation on the Defence under 65 ter (iii) that they indicate as to which ones they are objecting to and which ones they are not. And we would be pleased for any indication from them today as to -- if we can have the list of documents. I know there was a letter which had come to us, and we had asked Mr. Guenael of the Defence team to re-send it because -- for us to know which particular exhibits they are -- they are disputing. We have given them the exhibit list, Your Honour, and the source of all the documents, as to where each single document comes from, to assist them in this task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that this is not a practice of this Tribunal. I think during the cross-examination, if the Defence team has any doubts concerning of the authenticity of that document, they will ask some questions and challenge these documents. And you also have an opportunity to redirect your examination in which you could give some explanations on authenticity of those documents. So we'll see, you know, how many documents are you going to use through this -- this witness and what is the challenge by the Defence team during the proceedings. This is the only practice we adopted at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just indicate that after the break, when my learned friend furnishes the explanation that you asked her for, the Defence would seek to be heard and to make a submission at that time relating to the matters about which we spoke in the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your last name.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: My last name is Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And your first name?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Salko.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: With Your Honours' permission, I'll lead the witness on his personal particulars. I think the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were born on 25th September 1963; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your ethnic origin is a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were born in the hamlet -- I'll spell it out, P-i-j-e-s-a-k municipality.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: On 1st September 1979, you joined the military college in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the secondary military school.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Then you were sent to Belgrade to the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then you were in the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In 1986, you entered the military academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And in 1988, you graduated from this academy.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you were given the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a second lieutenant. That's the lowest officer's rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you for that. On 16th September 1991, you went to Knin in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were in the 9th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You acted as assistant to the battalion commander there.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In December 1991, you left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: November or December, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then you went to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, you returned to Sarajevo and joined the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Although, there were already contacts with them in November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: About April 1992, you were appointed to the position of the commander of the District TO Staff of the Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: That was the Regional Territorial Defence Staff Kosevsko Brdo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And at the end of May or the beginning of June 1992, you were appointed to the position of commander of the 11th Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In October 1992, you were the commander of the 1st Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: At the end of October 1992, you were appointed to the position of the commander of the Sarajevo TO District Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, the Sarajevo District Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And did this also mean that you were in charge of all TO units in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you were -- you were there at the staff headquarters until end of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You were then appointed to the position of the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade in Hrasnica. I'm sorry about the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I never actually took up that duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: On my arrival in Hrasnica, the brigade commander did not want to hand over his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: After this, I went to Igman and spent some time at Igman without any appointment. But very soon after that I was appointed commander of the 8th Motorised Brigade, and after that commander of the Igman Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And that was in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: From January to March, yes. The 28th of January until March. I don't know the exact day in March.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the -- what was the OG established to do?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The OG is a temporary military structure unifying more than one unit on a certain axis with a specific task relating to combat operations. The OG covered the territory of the municipalities of Hadzici, Trnovo, Hrasnica, and its task was to maintain communication with Gorazde. Apart from that, it was significant that within the OG was artillery providing support to the town which was besieged.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the OG directly subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The OG was subordinated to the command of the 1st Corps, headed by the late General Talijan. His name was Mustafa Hajrulahovic and he is deceased.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then in June 1993 you were appointed to the position of commander of the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I think it was on the 9th of June, 1993. I'm not absolutely sure, but I think it was the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Until what date did you retain this position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I was corps command until the 28th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What did you do after this date?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: After this date, for a while I was at the disposal of the staff of the Supreme Command, and then I was appointed head of the Department for Operative Command and Planning in the operations centre in the Supreme Command Staff in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What are you currently doing?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Currently I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So how long would that have made it that you were in the armed forces, Mr. Gusic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I was active for 22 years, including -- if you include my secondary schooling, then 26 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And you -- you were in two armed forces, were you not, the JNA and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that, in the JNA and the Army of BH. But I also had military schooling in Turkey from 1997 to 1999 in Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So during your career as a -- as a military -- as a senior military officer in the ABiH, you must have seen many documents, military documents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I also participated in compiling such documents. I personally drew up certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And is there a standard format which was used for issuing these documents?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there is. Every document in the left top corner has to have a heading including the name of the unit issuing the document. The document has to have a number and a date. On the right-hand side must be the degree of confidentiality of that document. Underneath has to be the subject matter, what the document refers to. On the right-hand side is the address of the addressee. Then the document has a preamble. Underneath the preamble, the type of document, whether it's an order, an instruction, a report, an announcement. Then there are the points of the order or report. On the right-hand side is the signature of the person issuing the order. And then on the left-hand side, all the addresses to which the document was sent to facilitate the distribution of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you would also be very familiar with the language used in these documents and the meaning of this language.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have command of that terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And if you were to see any document which emanated from the ABiH army, would you be in a position to identify the document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Because during the course of the testimony, Mr. Gusic, I will be showing you documents, and then at that point you will be asked to comment on it -- on them.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I think that should not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit 18, which is 00520767, which is MFI102.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honour. Your Honour, I will be giving the witness a B/C/S copy of this document. Usher, would you please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision on appointing me as the 6th Corps commander. And it's also a decision on appointing General Delic as commander of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This would be -- is it paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's coming up in the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And on the next page is when you're appointed as commander of the 6th Corps in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who else was appointed in this -- at the same time?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, under "4", it says -- there's the commander, Rasim Delic. He was appointed as the commander of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command. And then there are deputies who were appointed, Stjepan Siber, Jovan Divjak, and as Chief of the Main Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic was appointed to that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And on what date was this?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: This date isn't -- this document isn't quite the same as the usual ones. The 8th of June is in the left, and 1993. So it was on the 8th of June, 1993. That's at the bottom, to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Now, during your military career, how much training were you given with respect of aspects of international law regulating the conduct of war?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I received such education in my secondary school, at the academy, at the police -- military police course, at various courses and seminars organised in the unit. And when preparing myself for training with officers or troops and when using the relevant literature, I obtained such knowledge. So we continued to learn about that field. We consulted the laws issued by Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, the documents issued by them. These documents were difficult to obtain because they were frequently provided in electronic copies. It was usually a matter of reading them out in the presence of other officers. And when certain tasks were assigned, the duties regarding how war should be conducted were also referred to and respect for international conventions was also a matter that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So, in other words, commanders would be expected to know the law on the conduct of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't just say the commanders. All the officers in the former JNA and in the ABiH, because I don't think there were any officers who weren't familiar with those documents because there were such documents issued by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and all army members had the duty to read these documents. Every army member had the duty of being familiar with the basics.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were these soldiers given any training in this respect?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if your question concerns ABiH members, then not much training was given. It was -- they were usually trained in the course of moral preparations. But given the tasks and the situation in the battlefield, normal sort of training was not conducted during that period, 1992 and 1993, apart from the fact that documents were read out. But an organised form of training hadn't been put into place for the soldiers, or at least I'm not aware of such a system having been introduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So before you conducted any -- any military operation, would you talk to your soldiers before they went into combat?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that depended on the men to whom the task was being assigned. It depended on the level of the troops. When commanders were concerned, we'd talk to commanders. But the person leading the troops would speak to the troops about how the task was to be carried out. One of the issues to be discussed was how POWs and civilians and war booty should be treated, how men or people should be evacuated, as well as wounded. They also had to discuss supply routes, routes for the rotation of troops. So these were all matters that were discussed before going into combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you ever talk about civilians if the area of the military operation was going to be in an area where there would be civilians in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as civilians are concerned, I can't say that they were discussed as a separate factor. But objectives were selected. Tasks were assigned, tasks that had to be carried out. And I can claim with full responsibility that there was never a task assigned to me or to others that involved having civilian objectives or, rather, objectives, targets that were not military. And I'm not aware of anyone having ordered anything to be done of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was it the duty of the commanders to talk to the subordinates about how to treat civilians in the zone of combat?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The commander's duty was to talk to the soldiers about all the relevant subjects, and that included the subject you have mentioned too. And that's a commander's duty to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You said there were instructions and manuals which explained these matters.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were certain legal decisions, decrees, laws. There were certain rules which had been taken over to a large extent from the JNA, and they had been adapted to the conditions that prevailed and that the ABiH could accept.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to show you a document. And this is 00498463, 00498463. That's MFI103.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we please refer to Sanction, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I've never seen this order. Only the commander or the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command could have seen this order because the late Alija Izetbegovic, the president, drafted it. We in the units, subordinate units, must certainly have received orders on the basis of this order. And as far as I can see, in the title it says "The implementation of the law." Item 2, it says: "Commanders of armed forces and soldiers are bound to implement the rules of the International Laws of War." So item 2. I apologise. Item 2 in this order says: "Both commanders of armed forces and soldiers are bound to implement the rules of the International Laws of War. Commanders are duty-bound to inform their troops of these rules and ensure that they are respected," as I have said. We didn't have a sufficient copy of rules to distribute them to all the soldiers, but when the men were being prepared, such rules would be read out to inform the troops of the rules in force.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is a law signed by the President Izetbegovic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I would now like to show you 00137881, MFI104. Could you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: This is the Official Gazette from the ABiH. And in this gazette, on the first page "Instructions on the application of the international law" is provided for the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 4, please. Does it say that -- at paragraph 4 that "The following acts are war crimes," and it lists a number of crimes?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The war, genocide, the war against -- crimes against the civilian population, against the wounded, against patients, against medical staff, against prisoners of war, and other violations of the rules of war, such as killing or wounding an enemy who has surrendered, cruelly treating the wounded and the sick, killing without trial, et cetera. I can't comment on anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, basically you had instructions on the conduct of hostilities which all commanders and soldiers followed at the time of the war; is that correct? Would you consider that to be a correct position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But such a document could never be provided, not in this form. It could only be provided in an electronic version. We didn't have enough paper. And this is the first time I've seen a copy from the gazette. But it could be provided electronically, and then it would be printed in the unit and read out in the presence of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me the duties and responsibilities that you had as a 6th Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, as a corps commander, my first duty was to form a corps because the 6th Corps did not exist when I was appointed -- or until I was appointed as the commander. The next task was to carry out combat tasks in the area of responsibility of the corps. We also had to work on planning and drafting documents, making certain assessments, proposing certain operations, carrying out certain combat tasks that I could carry out without help from my superior command. I also had to take care of the logistics. We issued certain instructions for training, although the training wasn't as intensive as it should have been. We had a certain training centre, and when there were lulls in combat actions, certain men were trained. But this training was not sufficient. The main task on the whole was to organise and control -- or rather, conduct combat operations in the zone's AOR. I'm not going to mention all the rules which provide more specific information on all these tasks because I at the time did not have the occasion to consult such a rule book.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please now tell me, Mr. Gusic, what was the zone of responsibility of the 6th Corps. Can you tell me the municipalities which were under your area of control.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of the corps was divided into municipalities. I think that the first order referred to 12 municipalities, the municipality of Hadzici, Hrasnica, Trnovo, Kalinovik, Jablanica, Konjic, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Fojnica, Kresevo, Kiseljak, and Visoko. I think I have listed the 12 municipalities concerned. I think there were 12 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And whose zone of responsibility was Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Mostar was in the 4th Corps's zone of responsibility. The territory of the municipality of Mostar. I'm not just referring to the town of Mostar. And in my case, I was referring to the territory of the municipality, not just the central part of the municipality, not just the towns themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the 4th Corps's headquarters was where?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The 4th Corps headquarters was in Mostar. The corps headquarters was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was there access to Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict with HVO units, yes. After the conflict, there was access but it was difficult. The route went over the mountains. One had to bypass the roads. Footpaths had to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And in whose area of responsibility was Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: In the 4th Corps zone of responsibility, because that's the territory of the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, can you please now tell the Court what units were in the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll omit a unit or two, but I'll try to go on the basis of municipalities. Each municipality had a municipal staff. There was the Trnovo Municipal Staff, the Hadzici one, the Kiseljak, Kresevo, Fojnica, Konjic, Jablanica Municipal Staffs. Then there were the 43rd and 45th units, the 49th Brigade, and then the Fojnica Municipal Staff became the 310th Brigade. There was the 317th Brigade, the Gornji Vakuf Municipal Staff. I think that municipal staff had two detachments. In formal terms - when I say "formal" they were never really part of the corps, but according to the orders there were the Crni Labudovi, the Black Swans, and a few special purposes units, detachments for special purposes within the Supreme Command Staff. At the meeting in Zenica, I asked the commander to deal with the issue of these units because officially they were part of the corps but they were never actually part of the corps. I was never able to establish command over those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And was the Prozor Independent Battalion underneath the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The Prozor Battalion, yes. The municipal staff -- yes, there was the Independent Prozor Battalion that was part of the corps. There was also the 81st Brigade. I think I failed to mention that unit. There were a lot of units. I've probably forgotten to mention some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all right. And who was the commander of the Prozor Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Prozor Battalion at that period of time was Enver Buza.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the Zulfikar Unit. Under whose command was that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: That was a detachment for the special purposes within the Supreme Command Staff, and Zulfikar Alispago, Zuka, was the commander. For a certain period of time, this unit was deployed on Igman and it was later redeployed to the Jablanica area. It was a detachment for special purposes. I participated with that unit in combat; however, that unit was always tied to the Supreme Command Staff, and that was part of its title. It was called a special detachment which was within the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So was it ever under the 6th Corps command?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Officially, yes, on the basis of the orders issued, yes. But it was never actually under the corps command. Because this is an issue that I asked the commander at a meeting in Zenica to resolve, and after that meeting, after that briefing, the commander assigned that unit to the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And can you tell me if you know under whose command were the 9th and the 10th Brigades.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The 9th and 10th Brigades? They were within the 1st Corps, the Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And under who was the -- who was the -- who were they subordinate to, the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: To the Supreme Command Staff. At the time, to General Delic in 1993. After he was appointed, they were subordinated to General Delic. That was how the chain of command functioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Corps was General Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Were the 9th and 10th -- the 9th Motorised Brigade and the 10th Mountain Brigade attached to the Supreme -- the staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in September 1993, on the basis of an order from the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll come back --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I know that because it was on the basis of that order that it was my duty to take over the units in the Gradina area and to ensure that they could pass through to Jablanica. My subordinates took them over down there. I know that they had lunch in my command, and then we continued to Jablanica. All those units that had left Sarajevo continued to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what date this was?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was at the beginning of September. Perhaps it was on the 3rd or the 4th of September. They came to where I was located on the 3rd or 4th, and I think that the order was dated either the 2nd or the 3rd of September. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, 00520807, MFI105.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And may we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which they published the rules of service in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Such rules were also printed in the form of a green hardcover booklet, so I think that all brigade commanders had access to such a manual.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Other than at -- and this is going back a bit -- at paragraph 6, where you are -- there's general guidance on combat activities. And we already referred to this point, but this is yet another manual which tells you about how operations are to be conducted. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is just a rule that refers to the documents that you have already shown. This is just one item that refers to using those documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I want to use -- go to item 12. Are these the general principles of superior-subordinate relationships within the army?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These are rules -- were also in force, or similar ones were in force in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And they were completely followed in the -- in the ABiH army as well? They were adopted?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to paragraph 2 now, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: But I'd just like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, there were no ranks. Posts were indicated in a certain way. There were signs for corps commanders. There were signs that were similar to ranks. There were lilies that they had, but I think that ranks were introduced towards the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994. I think the first ranks appeared in December 1993. But this item was applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you look at -- from 15, 16. I think we'll have it in Sanction. Where it says "Carrying out the orders is the basis for successful life and work in the army and for completing existing tasks and duties of service." And 16 says: "The order of the superior commander, which is related to the service, must be carried out by any person serving in the army without discussion, completely, exactly and promptly."

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that's the case in all armies throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And this is how it was conducted in your army.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then it says that "Persons serving in the army must carry out orders of the most senior present commander, when the superior commander is absent and when it is necessary to take immediate measures for completing urgent tasks, especially in combat, in exceptional circumstances and under conditions of re-establishing damaged organisation of work, order and discipline."

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So would you say that inference from -- the direct order from that is that the more superior person in the field is authorised to issue orders in the absence of the commander?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only on the ground but the most senior person in terms of rank commands everybody, and that the same obtains on the ground. So in every place, wherever there is a senior officer present, he is always the one commanding the junior, less senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So as a -- as a corps commander, you were also authorised to issue binding orders to all officers in the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would this also include military security?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But I have to point out that they had a separate chain of command. We called them the security organs. And there was a chain of command from battalion level. A battalion had one security officer; a brigade had one with two other officers; the corps had an assistant commander for security; and then there was also a security administration at the level of the Supreme Command. And that was the chain of command used to issue orders which were very often something that the normal chain of command did not even know about. These were operations that they carried out which required a certain amount of secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But nevertheless, were you authorised to issue orders to the military security in your corps, despite this other chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And to the military intelligence and to the military police?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And were they duty-bound to carry out your orders?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Whose orders would you be bound by?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I was bound by the orders of the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, or orders issued by someone on his behalf. Very often there were orders signed by his deputies, General Siber, General Divjak, General Halilovic. There were orders like that which I was duty-bound to respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So what was the role over a deputy commander in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The deputy commander was a person who stood in for the commander and most often it was organised in almost all units so that he had authority over Territorial Defence units and staffs, but in the commander's absent, he stood in for the commander with reference to all areas and all issues. Because there has to be continuity of command in an army. The chain of command must never be broken. And this was ensured by having a deputy commander in every unit in the corps, at corps level, and not for a single moment could a unit be without a commander. If the commander was absent, the deputy would be there, who was authorised to issue orders on the commander's behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So the deputy commander could give binding orders to all lower-level military commanders, to himself.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. But he was also duty-bound to inform the commander that he had issued such orders in the shortest possible reasonable period of time. The commander had to be aware of what orders he had issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. But the -- the junior commander, the subordinates of the deputy commander, would have to listen to the orders of the deputy commander; is that the correct position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This order could only be challenged if two orders arrived at the same time, one issued by the commander and the other issued by his deputy. In that case, it would be the commander's order that would be followed, unless it contained elements that would constitute a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now document 023 -- oh, sorry, Your Honours. Can I go again? K0239566. And it's MFI106.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Are these --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: This is a chapter of the rules of the JNA, the rules on the work of commands and staffs. This was adopted by the Army of BH and used in its work. This is something that was very rarely available. The first time I saw it was in Kakanj in 1994, but this was used to issue instructions. This was used as a working document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can I take you to item 501, please, where it says that "Combat orders, commands, directives and instructions of general relevance and written approvals (authorisations) for representatives of the command are signed by the commander." That was the correct position in the army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say that "Reports of general relevance are signed by the commander and Chief of Staff." Further down on that paragraph, it says: "The Chief of Staff in his capacity as a deputy commander signs documents from the commander's jurisdiction only if the commander is not there and due to the urgency of the matter it is not possible to wait for his return." What does that tell you, Mr. Gusic? What do you understand by that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: What I have already said. In order to ensure continuity of command, the deputy commander -- or rather, in these rules the deputy commander is not mentioned, but the deputy commander or the Chief of Staff could sign documents on behalf of the commander due to the urgency of what was going on. In other words, they could issue combat orders or any kind of binding orders if the commander was not in a situation to sign them. And this was actually done on behalf of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what was the role of the Chief of Staff in the army?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was a professional organ belonging to the commander, and he was the most responsible officer for the organisation of the staff, all the staffs. And he was the one who compiled documents on assessments, preparing the forces, the way the units would be used. He made proposals to the commander regarding operations through his officers and organs, and he looked after all the staff work, all the staff jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who was your Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: My Chief of Staff was Dzevad Tirak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana, is it a proper time for us to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I promised to come back to you after the break about the question that you asked of the Prosecution, whether the witnesses were withdrawn on the confirmation list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let us continue with this witness, because, you know, it would be very awkward if we stop here and attend to something else. Maybe tomorrow morning -- tomorrow afternoon will be the -- before the witness came in we'll give you the opportunity to present your views on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. It's just that you enjoined me to come back to you after the break, and I was doing as I was asked. But I will continue now with the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, we were talking about the role of a deputy commander, and you'd just seen this document. Would it be fair to say, Mr. Gusic, that a deputy commander in the army could issue -- could authorise anyone in their corps to issue orders on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I raise an objection at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the objection is this, that the Defence is now baffled as to the way in which the Prosecutor is putting its case, and we think it ought to be clarified now. There are various ways in which Mr. Halilovic is said to have been in the position of commander of the troops, and this is a case which will ultimately require some analysis of the nature of command responsibility. So we need to know is the Prosecutor putting this case as one where he's commanding the troops in the exercise of his role as Chief of Staff, or the exercise of his role as deputy, or as a person appointed by an order or series of orders as a commander of a particular operation. And those matters, in my submission, ought to be clarified because otherwise this evidence is in danger of just being general evidence, not focussed upon -- upon the issues that there are. We've also understood that the Prosecution themselves have advanced the case that his responsibility is not purely based upon his -- role as a Chief of Staff. Therefore, these questions may -- and there's been many of them asked already -- may well have relevance and be justifiable, but the basis ought to be made clear, and in my submission can be purely and simply and quickly made clear now, and I'd ask that that be done, and that's the reason for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the fullness of time it will become evident to the Defence counsel as to what exactly this witness is going to be testifying about. By the end of his testimony, it will become clear that Mr. Gusic has also been asked to give general answers about the workings of the army doctrine -- military doctrine. Being a commander in the army, he's well equipped to answer such questions. And our case against the accused has been made very clear., that he is the effective commander of the troops which committed the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean there's no relevance for a deputy commander to issue orders, as the questioning addressed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This is equally relevant because the accused had many hats, Your Honour. He was a Chief of Staff and he was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this question put by the Prosecution to the witness is relevant to this case, and we'll see, you know, how things will go further. Maybe the Prosecution just to lay out the general background issues, try to show the command -- chain of commanders in the army. Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you as the commander, Mr. Gusic, authorise anybody in your corps to issue orders on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you also authorise a Chief of Staff, your Chief of Staff, to issue orders on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in Fojnica, there was a forward command post of the 6th Corps, and my Chief of Staff was the commander of that forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. I would now like to take you to what you know about investigations in the BH army. You were a commander, Mr. Gusic, of some seniority; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: In the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So you are aware of the procedures of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Every member of the army is aware of that, and especially those who had been active military men before the war, because there were not any big differences in relation to the JNA as regards discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You have also presumably had occasion to use these procedures yourself.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you then please tell the Chamber who was responsible for investigating and prosecuting war crimes in the BH army. I would ask you to be quite systematic, Mr. Gusic, when you inform the Chamber, and go one step at a time, and imagine now a war crime has been committed by a subordinate.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The commander of the unit who first learns of such an event is duty-bound to take steps at his level. These are most often squad or platoon commanders because they are in direct contact with the soldiers who might do such a thing. The squad or platoon commander would then be duty-bound to immediately inform the company commander. The company commander is an officer with more experience and more organs who can be tasked with this job. He can either go in person or send one of his officers to see what had happened, and then he would inform the battalion command. At that level, there would already be reporting according to two lines: One would be the security line; and the other one would be the chain of command and control. This information would then be transmitted up to the brigade command. The brigade command would be the first unit that would have men especially designated to deal with this. Those would be police companies. The brigade commander would then have to take the military police company to secure the place and to inform the corps command that this had happened. The corps would have military police battalions which would work in coordination with the Ministry of the Interior organs. In other words, if they did not have sufficient professional personnel, they would have to inform the MUP. They would then go to secure the place where the crime had taken place. They would have to take statements from men. And then the joint commander -- or rather, the staff of the Supreme Command would be informed, and it would be their duty to activate the military prosecutor's office. The military prosecutor and the investigating judge would be duty-bound to visit the scene of the crime, to carry out an on-site investigation, and the army units would assist the investigating judge by meeting his requests. If a member of the army had committed a crime, this person would have to be deprived of his liberty, detained. This was not prison but custody. According to our rules, commanders could detain someone between seven and ten days. The company commander would be able to do this for two days and then, depending on the level of the commander, the number of days would increase that they could keep someone detained. In the meantime, the investigating judge would hand down a decision on custody so that -- and all this would have to take not more than three days from the day the information was received. Then the investigating judge would continue his work according to his normal procedures.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So to be quite clear, so it was the military police who were responsible for investigating crimes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The military police had to secure the site, find clues. They would have to secure the place. But it would be the investigating judge who would actually carry out the investigation. In the army, we did not have people who were able to carry out an investigation professionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's quite so. And just in order for -- for the Chamber to be quite clear on the matter: So the military police investigate, and then the military investigative judge investigated the crime as well. It went to the investigative judge after that.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And on whose orders would the military police act in the investigation of this crime?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The officer -- it could be the brigade police, the brigade commander. And if it was the police at the corps level, it would be the corps commander. The security organs were professional units, and the security organ could order the use of the unit for such things. He could not use them in combat, but he could issue the order in order to do their job, their professional job.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So the military police would act on the orders of the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Out on the ground, yes. But it would be the commander or the security organ sending the military police out onto the ground. When they got there, the investigating judge would issue the orders, and the military police would have to do as he told them to.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what rules and regulations and the law would the investigative judge follow in the conduct of his investigations?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the laws and other legislation regulating these matters. The prosecutor's office had their own regulations. I have to admit I wasn't fully familiar with those. But there were districts. Every district had its own prosecutor's office -- military prosecutor's office, and those were Sarajevo, Mostar, Tuzla, I think, Zenica. I don't know if there were any others. There were probably more. Those are the four military prosecutor's offices that I knew existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: All right. Now, the scene of the crime has been secured by the military police. What happens next?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: When the military police secures the scene, they must make sure that nothing is moved. Then the investigating judge arrives, and he carries out the procedures he has to perform. Those persons who are suspects, if the unit is aware of that, the unit commander takes steps to detain that person. Otherwise, the investigating judge issues a warrant. This is all done under the supervision of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would the civilian police in any way assist the military?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: The civilian police most often assisted, because we did not have enough professionals in the army, and the civilian police always gave us professional assistance at the request of a command at any level. For example, in the area of responsibility of the 6th Corps, there was an example where the civilian police of the municipality of Fojnica carried out and completed an investigation. This was when the friars in the Fojnica monastery were murdered. The military police only helped by identifying the perpetrators, but the whole process of carrying out the investigation, finding the accused, this was done by the Ministry of the Interior of Fojnica, headed by the chief of police. His name was Sead Mackic. This was the person who carried out the investigation. And he was the chief of police in Fojnica, of the civilian police. This was just an example to illustrate my point. And this could be done with any chief of police in any town or village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So would -- could you tell us: Whose responsibility was it to initiate these criminal investigations within the -- the army? Whose responsibility was it?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to specific cases?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: That -- in general, the investigation was initiated by the commanders at every level. It was their duty to initiate an investigation, but it differed depending on their level. It was a platoon commander who did the least; the company commander would do more. Then the brigade commander would do even more. So the further up you went, the more could be done. The Supreme Command was the highest level, and they already had contact with the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So up the chain of command it was the responsibility of every commander along the line.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of every commander and of every army member. Because according to the rules we had, it's not only the commanders that had such duties but all army members had such duties too. But in any event, the commander was the person who bore the greatest amount of responsibility in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you have any instructions or manuals or any directives saying this?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: There were instructions, legal instructions issued by the Republic of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, by the Supreme Command Staff, and these instructions were forwarded to the lowest levels. They were received via the chain of command or they were received through the professional line from the Security Services. The interpretation of these rules also went via the organ for morale, or rather, in the organ for morale within the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I want to show you a document, please, now, which is 00520821, MFI107.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: These are the rules on military discipline.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an Official Gazette in which rules on military discipline were published.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before I ask you to go to a specific page, was there a difference between initiating investigations during peacetime and wartime in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course there was a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So different rules applied.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And I will take you now to Section 5, "Establishment of disciplinary accountability during a state of war." It starts at Article 67. Article 67 basically says that these rules shall be applied accordingly in a state of war. 67 says: "Decisions on disciplinary accountability or breaches of military discipline during a state of war shall be taken as a matter of urgency." And 69 defines that urgency as 24 hours. Was that the position that you followed?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, if it was urgent, it had to be dealt with within three days. It wasn't a problem to do if there was a three-day period. But when a matter was urgent, in all military documents, the time period was three days unless otherwise stated. But if it could be dealt with in -- within 24 hours, that was the most efficient way to proceed. But in wartime it's very difficult to respect this time limit, so they would usually try to deal with matters within a three-day period.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Article 71 is where it refers to the three days.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I didn't even have a look at that. While during a state of war, yes, that's the rule that the army applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, why is that the case? Why do you have to take immediate measures during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, measures must urgently be taken in a state of war to ensure that negative incidents did not spread, to prevent such incidents in units and to preserve the system of command and control. In very tense situations, if you do not react to a certain incident, this can have a very negative influence on everyone, on all the troops, and this is why it is important to act immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: You as a commander, were you equally responsible to ensure that you would be informed of war crimes committed by your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And how would you ensure that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Through subordinate commanders or through the professional organs within the command. Or if I was on the site, then by carrying out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No. But what was the established form by which commanders were informed of possible breaches? What -- how would you be informed? You're everywhere. You're in a war zone.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Through the chain of command, from commanders, platoon commanders, company commanders, battalion commanders, brigade commanders. So it would be forwarded through the usual chain that would be used to report on events. Officers and subordinate units had the duty to forward such information to their superiors as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was it in writing? Was it verbally? Was it by your -- your radio communications?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: As far as the chain of command is concerned, well, it was forwarded in writing. But within the command itself, if someone -- if the professional organs of the command were concerned, they could relay the information orally. But it was their duty to provide a report on any exceptional events. So this was one form in which they would report on exceptional events. It was necessary to have a written trace, written documents on the event in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What were the communications like at that time? How were you communicating with each other in the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult. Communications were very difficult. Communications in the ABiH were very complicated, or rather, our communications equipment was not of a very high standard. Usually we had a stationary radio post, and these radio posts were usually located at the command posts of certain units, so that the information one could receive by using that means was only information you could use when you were in the vicinity of the command post or in the command post itself. There were very few mobile stations that commanders could take with them and that would enable them to have communications at all points in time. So usually we had to rely on the stationary communication posts which were located at command posts. But if the equipment functioned, given the conditions that prevailed, we did have a system of communications. We did receive information. I can't say that it was always received in good time, but it was possible to carry out the tasks assigned by using these -- by using this system of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But there was an existing and a functional communications system. Difficult though it may have been.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What if it was a matter of some urgency, like you're -- you're away from your post at that time and there are some crimes being committed. Immediately you need to be informed. What were -- what were the procedures you set up with your subordinates who were left in charge?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, command and control is a permanent duty and function, so there was always someone who had the authority to command and there was always someone who was authorised to receive such information and take the necessary measures. If the commander wasn't present, the deputy commander was there or the Chief of Staff. If the Chief of Staff wasn't there, then there would be someone appointed by the commander or there would be the most senior commander in the brigade. One always knew who was responsible to take certain measures. One always knew the identity of those replacing other officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But in such times, would you be -- would you have put into place procedures where you'd be immediately informed, as soon as practically and possible, of course?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. If an officer was in the territory under the control of the ABiH, the information was often relayed through neighbouring communications centres, and at the bottom of such documents it usually stated that we are requesting that our colleagues from such-and-such a centre forward this information to such-and-such a person. So at the bottom of the document, there was always such a message typed out by the communications officials. I can't say that it was extremely efficient, but it was the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What if -- what if it came to pass that you did not know who the perpetrators were in a particular crime which had been committed? What was the procedure then for a commander?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, the security organs tried to gather information that might indicate the identity of the perpetrator of such a crime, and most frequently they used their associates in army units or outside the army to obtain such information, which they would then forward to those within the system of command and control so that this information could be processed. If something like that happened, it wasn't only the responsibility of the army. The MUP and other structures, security structures, would get involved too.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What resources were at your disposal as a commander when you conducted investigations or indeed any commander in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to? The activities of the military police, of the communications service, activities involving combat action? What are you referring to exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: To investigations. Well, the means were very poor. The equipment we had was a little obsolete. We had some equipment in Konjic in the police department. I'm referring to the 6th Corps. There wasn't that much equipment. But there was cooperation at the highest level with MUP units, and their equipment was better and they would provide us with that equipment in such situations, and that is what the chief of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, did in Fojnica, and he successfully conducted that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who were the investigative judges in the area at the time, in your area of operations.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC
utterances.text: I know that at the time he was called Bahrudin Comor. The judge was Bajric -- I can't remember his first name. But I think the investigating judge was Comor. I think he was the investigating judge, Bahrudin Comor. I'm not a hundred percent sure. I know about this because on one occasion they conducted an investigation into me, and I think that Bajric was the judge in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Before I leave this subject of military discipline, there is one document I'd like to show you, and this is in respect of what your earlier answer had been that deputy commanders had the authority to issue -- I mean, sorry, a commander could authorise deputy commanders to issue binding orders. It is 00554735, MFI108, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just raise a matter. It's related to the previous objection but different to it. I'll just remind the Court that on the 24th of January, 2005 counsel appearing for the Prosecutor - at that time Mr. Re - said this -- and this is at page 14, line 1. He said: The exhibits on our exhibit list, the pre-trial brief; both versions, the notice we gave to the Defence in Chambers, in the purported supplement to the pre-trial brief -- he said some other things -- the Prosecution maintains -- it's still notice to the Defence as to the legal case theory. We do concede the last portion, the last paragraph of the motion filed today in relation to paragraph 207. And the accused's alleged responsibility as a deputy commander of the army. We concede - I'll say it straight up right now - that what's in the pre-trial brief is incorrect. Now, Your Honour ruled on the previous objection. This is a more specific line of questioning, and it's revisiting that area.
